1.title: Know the farm, the seasons and the words
1.intro: Farming turns land, water, seed or animals, and work into food or fibre. Start with the basic words and the yearly cycle.
pts: Learn the terms: crop, livestock, yield, input, soil test, rotation, harvest, grade.
Canada has short growing seasons in many regions, so timing matters.
Know the main farm types: field crops, vegetables and fruit, dairy, beef, poultry, greenhouse.
Visit a farm or market and ask what the hardest month is and why.
1.ex: Yield: 3 tonnes per hectare means three tonnes harvested from each hectare planted.
1.act: Visit or interview one farmer. Write a one-page summary of the farm type, the main inputs and the yearly calendar.
1.std: Task: write a farm summary. Condition: from one visit or interview. Standard: terms used correctly, a calendar of the year, and the main input costs named.

2.title: Explain how a crop or animal product gets from plan to sale
2.intro: The chain has steps. If you see them, you can find where money and time are lost.
pts: Steps: plan, prepare, plant or start, care, harvest, store, sell.
Each step has inputs (seed, feed, fuel, labour) and a risk (weather, disease, price).
Keep a field or animal record: dates, amounts, treatments, weather notes.
Know your market before you plant: who buys, in what size, at what time.
2.ex: A small vegetable farm plants lettuce every two weeks so that it can sell weekly to a restaurant buyer, not all at once.
2.act: Draw the chain for one product from seed to buyer and mark where it could fail.
2.std: Task: draw a production chain. Condition: for one product you could grow or raise. Standard: all steps shown with at least one input and one risk per step.

3.title: Carry out a basic farm task to a standard
3.intro: Do one real task with care: for example, a soil sample, seeding a bed, or a daily animal check.
pts: Follow a written method and keep a record of what you did and when.
Measure results, such as germination rate, weight gain or yield per bed.
Use tools and machines safely; get trained before using any machine.
Compare the result with your goal and write one change for next time.
3.ex: Germination rate = seeds that sprouted divided by seeds planted. 90 of 100 seeds sprouted: 90 percent.
3.act: Complete one growing or care task twice, record the results and improve the second run.
3.std: Task: do one core task twice. Condition: small scale, supervised by an experienced grower. Standard: written method, measured result, and second run is better.

4.title: Follow food, land and workplace rules
4.intro: Farm rules come from federal, provincial and local governments. Find which apply before you sell or hire.
pts: Food safety: food that is sold across provinces or exported has federal rules; local sales follow provincial and public health rules. Check which apply to you.
Chemicals and fertilizer: rules on licences, storage and use differ by province. Check with the provincial agriculture office.
Workers: employment standards and workplace safety rules apply on farms; farm rules differ by province. Check the current rules.
Some products such as milk, eggs and poultry have quota or marketing board systems. Learn this before you plan to enter those sectors.
4.ex: Rules table row: 'Selling eggs at the farm gate | provincial agriculture office | check grading and registration rules | before the first sale | written reply kept'.
4.act: Build a rules table for your product and province with the enforcer, the action and the date checked.
4.std: Task: make a rules table. Condition: using official public pages or a call to the provincial office. Standard: no rule is guessed; each row has a dated source.

5.title: Work out costs, price and profit
5.intro: A farm that does not cover its costs closes. Count every cost, including your own time.
pts: Variable costs: seed, feed, fuel, packing. Fixed costs: land payment or rent, insurance, equipment, loan interest.
Cost per unit = total cost divided by units produced.
Margin per unit = price minus cost per unit. Break-even = fixed cost divided by margin per unit.
Check programs that share risk, such as crop or income support. Check current terms with the agriculture office.
5.ex: A bed of carrots costs 300 CAD to grow and gives 600 kg. Cost is 0.50 per kg. Sold at 2.00 per kg the margin is 1.50 per kg. Teaching figures only.
5.act: Build a cost sheet for one crop or animal group and compute break-even.
5.std: Task: build a cost sheet. Condition: with real local input prices. Standard: units shown, formulas visible, three what-if cases such as a 20 percent lower yield.

6.title: Run daily work and keep records
6.intro: Farms succeed through steady habits and good records.
pts: Make a weekly calendar of tasks and a daily checklist.
Keep records of inputs, treatments, harvest, sales and waste.
Plan storage and cold chain so food stays safe and fresh.
Review the numbers monthly: yield, cost, waste, cash.
6.ex: Weekly page: harvested 120 kg, sold 105 kg, waste 15 kg (12.5 percent). Action: pick earlier in the morning and cool faster.
6.act: Run a four-week log on a small plot or animal group and choose one improvement.
6.std: Task: keep a four-week log. Condition: real small-scale production. Standard: weekly entries complete; the improvement is dated and its result noted.

7.title: Sell your product and build buyers
7.intro: Know who buys, how they find you and what they need.
pts: Routes: farm gate, markets, box programs, restaurants and shops, and co-operatives.
Write a one-page offer: product, quality, quantity, price, delivery, how to order.
Label honestly; follow packaging and language rules for your product. Check the current rules.
Keep a list of buyers and a calendar for contacting them.
7.ex: A farm offers 'weekly box of eight vegetables, pick-up Saturday, 30 CAD, order by Wednesday'.
7.act: Contact fifteen possible buyers and get five replies. Record price, size and timing wanted.
7.std: Task: run a buyer search. Condition: two weeks. Standard: contacts logged, replies recorded, one change made to the offer.

8.title: Manage risk, run a season and plan growth
8.intro: Weather, disease and price swings are certain. Plan for them and then run a whole season.
pts: Risk register: weather, pests, disease, equipment failure, price drop, injury, theft, with controls and owners.
Keep insurance, backup water and power, and a cash buffer.
Respect land and water; protect soil and local wildlife; ask Indigenous neighbours and elders about local practices where invited.
Run a pilot season, write the review and a 12-month plan.
8.ex: Stop rule: 'If less than half the expected carrots can be sold by day 60, we change the buyer plan.'
8.act: Write the risk register of eight rows, run the pilot, and present the review to a panel.
8.std: Task: run a pilot season and review. Condition: real production with written measures. Standard: decisions follow the numbers; panel can repeat the plan.

quiz: What is yield?
The amount harvested per unit of land or per animal.
How do you work out germination rate?
Seeds that sprouted divided by seeds planted.
Why record dates, amounts and treatments?
To prove what you did, learn from it and meet rules.
Who do you ask about chemical use rules?
The provincial agriculture office.
What is cost per unit?
Total cost divided by units produced.
How is break-even found?
Fixed cost divided by margin per unit.
Which farm products often use quota or marketing boards?
Milk, eggs and poultry; check local rules.
Why keep a cold chain?
To keep food safe and fresh.
Name three routes to sell farm products.
Farm gate, markets, box programs, restaurants, shops or co-operatives.
What do you do when you do not know a rule?
Ask the official office and keep the answer in writing.
